newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Cosatu threatens new strike in 14 days.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Cosatu threatens new strike in 14 days.

text.p: Failure by business to respond to labour's demands over new employment legislation within 14 days would lead to renewed strike action, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) said on Monday.

"The ball is now firmly in the court of the employers. We expect them to respond with revised proposals either directly or through the National Economic Development and Labour Council," Cosatu general secretary Sam Shilowa told a news conference.
Shilowa said Cosatu expected the Business South Africa employers group to come back with revised proposals within 14 days, otherwise there would be a continuation of strike action.

Cosatu called a 24-hour stayaway on Monday and said two million workers had responded. Of these 1.6 million belonged to Cosatu affiliated unions and the balance were either affiliated to the National Council of Trade Unions or unaffiliated.
The strike was the third national stoppage since the 1994 elections which President Nelson Mandela's government to power.
Assistant general secretary Zwelinzima Vavi said the federation's executive committee would meet on June 24 to set a deadline for the conclusion of negotiations within Nedlac.

"We want to put a deadline on talks and review our programme of action in relation to negotiations," he said, noting talks in Nedlac over the labour legislation have been going on since April last year.
"If they (business) want to go for a war of nerves we are ready for them," said Shilowa.
"We are willing to take business on for the success of workers' issues...and we make no apologies."
South African business said support for Monday's one-day national strike had proved limited and many employers had made contingency plans which had minimised the impact.
But Shilowa said it was clear the majority of workers backed Cosatu in its stance on the planned Basic Conditions of Employment Bill.
"There's no doubt that workers stand full-square behind the position put forward by Cosatu," Shilowa said.

The bill, approved by cabinet in April, sets a 45-hour working week and four months maternity leave. Cosatu, the biggest union federation with 1.9 million members, wants a 40-hour week, six months maternity leave and the minimum age for formal employment to be set at 18.
